item.title: PEOPLE I Faithful to the call
item.description: FOR more than four decades, Peni Senikarawa Tamanisau has dedicated his working life to the Seventh-day Adventist Church. A native of Nayavu, Wainibuka, Tailevu, Peni is now responsible for looking after the church-owned sprawling Fulton Tailevu property.
item.content:encoded:
FOR more than four decades, Peni Senikarawa Tamanisau has dedicated his working life to the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

A native of Nayavu, Wainibuka, Tailevu, Peni is now responsible for looking after the church-owned sprawling Fulton Tailevu property.

The once-bustling college campus is now largely vacant. Only four staff quarters are occupied, along with two churches — one serving the Hindi-speaking congregation and the other the iTaukei-speaking worshippers.

Yet for Peni, the stillness of the property does not mean there is little to do.

His responsibilities include maintaining the grounds and buildings, ensuring the property is secure, keeping the surroundings clean and attending to the general upkeep of the site. He is supported by three casual workers who assist him with the demanding work.

Peni approaches his responsibility with the same dedication that has characterised his long association with the Church.

“I like my work because it is executed in a place that is stress-free and full of peace and quiet,” he says.

Peni completed his secondary education at Fulton College in 1989. He later joined the maintenance section of the college, where he worked from 1993 until late 2013, when the institution relocated to its new home in Sabeto, Nadi.

His connection with Fulton Tailevu, however, never really ended.

At the end of 2023, Peni returned to the old campus, this time as its caretaker. Fulton Tailevu was once a vibrant centre of education, drawing students from across the South Pacific. Young people from different island nations came to Fiji to study, live and prepare themselves for service in their communities.

For Peni, caring for such a large and mostly empty property requires more than simply turning up for work.

“You have to like what you do in order to be faithful to the job,” he says.

His commitment is rooted in something deeper than employment.

“Since leaving high school at Fulton College in 1989, I knew I was going to work for the church that educated me and taught me discipline and moral values.”

That sense of calling has sustained him through the years.

“I felt like working for an institution run by the church was my calling, and four decades later I am still here.”

His words reflect a life in which work and faith have become closely intertwined.

“I remained faithful because God has remained faithful to me. I would be earning more if I worked elsewhere, but I currently am satisfied with what I do because I know I would gain more in the long run.”

item.title: PEOPLE | Lessons from the price tag | Former SVC head girl shares real-world money advice
item.description: When Priyanka Mishra returned to Brisbane’s shopping centres after her graduation ceremony, she found herself doing something she had never really done before. Every price tag became a mental calculation.
item.content:encoded:
When Priyanka Mishra returned to Brisbane’s shopping centres after her graduation ceremony, she found herself doing something she had never really done before.

Every price tag became a mental calculation.

Thirty Australian dollars? That was about $F70. Did she really need it?

“Most of the time, I’d quietly put it back on the shelf,” she said.

It was a small habit born out of living on her own savings and one that has shaped her understanding of financial literacy.

Returning to her former school, Swami Vivekananda College, as chief guest at its Financial Literacy Awards, the 2018 head girl shared lessons not drawn out of textbooks, but from personal experience.

She reminded students that everyone’s financial journey is different.

While some receive pocket money, others juggle part-time work or help support their families.

Because circumstances differ, financial success is not measured by income but by the choices people make.

“It’s not about how much money you have, but about the decisions you make with what you have.”

Priyanka also urged students to avoid comparing themselves with others, particularly on social media.

Having stepped away from Instagram two years ago, she said she grew tired of the constant pressure to keep up with carefully curated versions of other people’s lives.

“Comparison is a race nobody ever truly wins, so run your own race and trust your own journey.”

Financial literacy should not mean denying yourself every enjoyment, instead it is about making deliberate choices.

She shared the story of saving for a bungy jump in Queenstown, New Zealand, an experience she had dreamed about for years.

Rather than spending impulsively, she planned and saved until she could afford it.

“I’ll always remember standing on that bridge before taking that leap,” she said, describing it as money well spent on a lifelong memory.

Now working full-time, Priyanka automatically sets aside part of every pay cheque for savings and has begun investing to build for the future.

She does not claim to have mastered personal finance.

“But I realised something – future Priyanka deserves a little help from present Priyanka.”

item.title: PEOPLE I Beyond the menu
item.description: For chef Asupa Leba, creating memorable meals isn’t about expensive ingredients or elaborate techniques. It’s about telling the story of a place through its food.
item.content:encoded:
For chef Asupa Leba, creating memorable meals isn’t about expensive ingredients or elaborate techniques.

It’s about telling the story of a place through its food.

The Totoya, Lau native is the culinary force behind the newly renovated Tailevu Hotel in Korovou, where she is introducing a menu inspired by the rich flavours and produce of Tailevu.

Her journey into hospitality began at the Shangri-La Fijian Resort on the Coral Coast before she refined her craft in some of Suva’s popular cafés and coffee houses.

While those years exposed her to modern dining, it was Korovou that inspired her biggest challenge yet.

“I walked around town to see what people were eating,” Ms Leba said.

“I realised there wasn’t a place where families could enjoy affordable fine dining in a beautiful setting. That’s what inspired this menu.”

That philosophy is evident throughout her carefully curated breakfast, lunch and dinner offerings.

From a hearty big breakfast to a colourful catch-of-the-day platter featuring crispy fried fish, stuffed freshwater mussels, kokoda, miti ota, tuna-filled rourou balls and eggplant fritters, every dish celebrates locally grown vegetables and freshly caught seafood.

For dinner, traditional favourites such as succulent sui served with rourou or moca, alongside fish simmered in rich coconut cream, showcase the comforting flavours that have long been part of Fijian family tables.

For Ms Leba, the menu is about more than satisfying hungry travellers.

It is her contribution to lifting the standard of dining in Korovou while creating opportunities for local farmers and fishermen whose produce fills her kitchen each day.

As Tailevu Hotel begins a new chapter, Chef Asupa Leba proves that some of Fiji’s finest dining experiences can be found when served with genuine hospitality and a deep respect for local flavours.

Tailevu Hotel chef, Asupa Leba, prepares her famous catch of the day. Picture: JOHN KAMEA

item.title: PEOPLE I Roadside dreams
item.description: DREAMS are not only born in classrooms and offices. If the mind is willing, prosperity can also be founded on a dusty roadside.
item.content:encoded:
DREAMS are not only born in classrooms and offices.

If the mind is willing, prosperity can also be founded on a dusty roadside.

For the past one month, Maria Luisa, mother of two, has been starting work as early as 6am, arranging bundles of fresh vegetables at her roadside stall, waiting for the day’s first customers.

To passing motorists, it may seem like just another roadside market.

But for the mother of two, every sale represents a chance to pay household bills, put food on the table and invest in her children’s future.

Maria never imagined the roadside would become her workplace.

Having left school early and struggled to find stable employment, she knows what it feels like to be judged by circumstances beyond her control.

Today, however, she has a different message for others facing similar challenges.

“Dropping out of school and being unemployed should not define you,” she said.

Just a month ago, Maria opened her small roadside business, selling fresh farm produce to earn an income for her family.

“I am doing this not for any grand purpose,” she said.

“I just want to help with the family’s daily expenses and bills.”

Like many small business owners, Maria’s week follows a predictable routine.

Tuesdays begin before sunrise as she travels to the Nausori and Suva markets to buy fresh produce from wholesalers.

By the end of the week, her roadside stall is stocked with vegetables ready for loyal customers.

Fridays and Saturdays are her busiest days, often bringing in more than $100 in sales.

Although she sometimes feels shy about working by the roadside, she refuses to let self-doubt stand in her way.

“My children are the reason I am doing this—nothing more, nothing less,” she said.

“I hope they will be successful and achieve more than I have.”

Before becoming her own boss, Maria worked as a supermarket cashier.

While the job provided a regular income, she says nothing compares to the flexibility of running her own business from home.

“I have access to cash every day, and I can finish work whenever I want. I can be my own boss.”

Maria believes there are many opportunities for stay-at-home mothers to earn an income by making the most of the resources around them.

“Not having an office job should not define you,” she said.

“Use whatever resources you have around you to earn a little extra income.”

Her advice is for anyone who believes their lack of education or employment has closed the door to success.

“Always believe you can succeed, even if you left school early or don’t have a job.”

item.title: PEOPLE | Halofaki stands firm | A guardian for women and tradition
item.description: After dedicating 42 years of her life to government service, spending 38 of those years working across Fiji’s remote maritime regions, Rigieta Halofaki retired in 2019. However, the president of the Soqosoqo Vakamarama iTaukei in the province Lau says her most critical battle actually began after she left office.
item.content:encoded:
After dedicating 42 years of her life to government service, spending 38 of those years working across Fiji’s remote maritime regions, Rigieta Halofaki retired in 2019.

However, the president of the Soqosoqo Vakamarama iTaukei in the province Lau says her most critical battle actually began after she left office.

It is the relentless fight to protect the indigenous women of the Lau Group from having their cultural intellectual property stolen.

For generations, Lauan women have woven intricate mats, beaten delicate masi (tapa cloth), and created unique traditional designs distinct to their home islands. Today, these heritage designs are being exploited for commercial profit with zero financial return to the rural women who created them.

“It is mostly the Lauan women affected because they are the ones who consistently maintain our handicraft traditions and culinary preparation,” Mrs Halofaki said.

“Nowadays, a great deal of this handicraft making is being heavily abused for commercial gain by outsiders.”

Speaking at the inaugural Lau Intellectual Property Awareness Workshop in Suva, Mrs Halofaki highlighted glaring local examples that have fueled her frustration. She pointed out that major local home centers are frequently replicating distinct Lauan motifs onto commercial products without authorisation.

“One recent example is businesses using our traditional prints to manufacture items for sale. They are simply not supposed to do that.”

An even more distressing trend involves the unauthorised replication of sacred Lauan designs onto commercial floor carpets sold openly in retail shops.

“A company imports these from a manufacturer and supplies them to local home centers. Our cultural designs are being printed right onto floor carpets.

“If they wished to utilise our patterns, they should have formally sought permission from the indigenous women, because those designs belong to them.”

The exploitation, she notes, extends deeply into the supply chain. Middlemen routinely travel to the maritime islands to buy prized handicrafts from local women at a low, fixed “standard price,” only to retail the items in Suva at three to four times the original cost.

“It is the middlemen who are unjustly benefiting. They purchase the items cheaply and flip them for immense profit. In essence, they are stealing from the women of Lau.

“The rightful benefits must go directly to the artisans who physically create the handicrafts, not to exploitative intermediaries.”

This cultural crisis is not a new grievance. Mrs Halofaki revealed that the Soqosoqo Vakamarama iTaukei has been lobbying the Solicitor-General and Attorney-General’s offices for the past five years to secure legal protections.

“It is an honor to host this workshop because this has been an ongoing discussion for five years, yet it feels as though no one has taken it far enough to be legally legislated.”

The workshop aimed to break that cycle of inaction. Women from across the Lau Group and the Suva diaspora unified to demand robust legislation protecting traditional knowledge and indigenous intellectual property. A draft bill addressing these gaps is anticipated to be tabled in Parliament this September.

For Mrs Halofaki, the push is about safeguarding a living legacy rather than just passing a law.

“We must carry on this legacy. Many of our mothers and grandmothers have passed away. If we do not actively preserve this traditional knowledge and pass it on to the generations coming up behind us, we will lose it entirely.”

Recognising her platform, she views her post-retirement role with absolute clarity.

“We are their mouthpiece. The women on the islands rely on us to stand up and fight for what they have been struggling to protect for years.”

If the proposed intellectual property legislation successfully passes through Parliament, she believes it will mark a historic turning point for maritime artisans.

“If that legislation is passed, it will be a momentous celebration for our women.”

Until that day comes, the intricate weaving continues on the islands—and so does the fight in the capital.

Rigieta Halokafi says middlemen routinely travel to the maritime islands to buy prized handicrafts from local women at a low, fixed “standard price,” only to retail the items in Suva at three to four times the original cost.

Rigieta Halofaki fights relentlessly to protect the indigenous women of the Lau Group from having their cultural intellectual property stolen. Picture: JULIA VADEI

item.title: PEOPLE | Family and hard work
item.description: THE pride in Satish Chand’s voice is unmistakable, but it is the tears that tell the real story. As the 72-year-old from Nabilo settlement, in Tailevu, talks about his five children he pauses — overcome with emotion.
item.content:encoded:
THE pride in Satish Chand’s voice is unmistakable, but it is the tears that tell the real story.

As the 72-year-old from Nabilo settlement, in Tailevu, talks about his five children he pauses — overcome with emotion.

Decades of hard work and careful planning have given way to a quiet satisfaction as he watches the family he and his wife built thrive, with children now working across Fiji, Australia and Papua New Guinea.

Mr Chand is a livestock farmer who sells vegetables at the Korovou Town market.

Mr Chand said nothing could compare to the struggles they endured and successfully overcame together.

For him, the market is part of a daily schedule but behind his familiar smile is a lifetime of sacrifice that has helped shape the future of the family he treasures most.

“I come to the market at six o’clock in the morning and I leave at five in the afternoon.

“Because I have livestock, I always get up as early as 3:30am. I always feed my cattle, ducks, goats, chickens, dogs and even the cats, and after that I come to the market.”

His working day does not end when he returns home.

“When I return, I make sure to check up on them again before I rest.”

The discipline has become second nature after years of caring for the animals.

Nothing on the farm goes to waste. Unsold vegetables from the market become feed for his animals, allowing him to make use of everything he has.

Before becoming a market vendor Mr Chand worked as a carpenter and later worked at the Veisama Rice Mill in Nausori, but realised he needed a better plan.

“After I left my job at the rice mill, I came to the market to sell.

The decision has allowed him to remain active while enjoying the company of fellow vendors.

“Here, I meet people. It’s basically a hobby for me and we help each other.”

Although he enjoys the work, it is family that gives his life its deepest meaning.

When talking about his five children, his voice softens and emotion fills the conversation.

He and his wife started their family after moving away from his parents’ home, determined to build a life of their own.

Today, that family’s achievements are his greatest reward.

“We have five children. I have two daughters in Australia, one son is an accountant in PNG, my fourth daughter is a schoolteacher and my last one works in Korovou.”

As he speaks about them, pride quickly gives way to emotion.

The success they have found is something he never takes for granted.

His joy has only grown with the arrival of grandchildren.

“I’m happy with my grandchildren and I like it when they visit and when they call daily.”

Despite having children living overseas, Mr Chand has never been tempted to leave the place he has always called home.

“My children have always asked if I could one day see myself living abroad. I told them I preferred the life here.”

“My parents used to live in Kuku in Nausori and also at Rabulu, but they moved here to farm.

“When they got here, they bought freehold land and that was where our lives started.

Those strong family values continue to guide him every day, especially in the way he cares for his wife, who has battled an illness for many years.

item.title: PEOPLE I A family of captains – Barotu’s first woman boat captain
item.description: Every morning begins the same way for Katarina Vunisa: she does all the house chores, checks the tide, walks down to the boat and prepares for the day’s crossing. At 51, she is the first woman in Barotu, Ra to hold a boat captain’s licence, a role she did not plan for but has grown into with confidence.
item.content:encoded:
Every morning begins the same way for Katarina Vunisa: she does all the house chores, checks the tide, walks down to the boat and prepares for the day’s crossing.

At 51, she is the first woman in Barotu, Ra to hold a boat captain’s licence, a role she did not plan for but has grown into with confidence.

Vunisa is originally from Taveuni, where boats were simply how people got around. She grew up travelling by sea from childhood, long before she ever imagined she would one day captain her own.

“I am someone fond of the ocean,” Vunisa said.

“In my village in Taveuni, boat ride was the only mode of transportation, hence being a boat captain seemed natural.

“Boat captains always piqued my interest as a little girl,” she added.

Barotu, where she has lived since, sits on the roadside in Ra, a village like many others along the coast.

What set her apart from her neighbours was not just where she was from, but the seven to 10-minute boat ride she came to take several times a week, ferrying women from the village to the mangrove restoration site under the Kiwa RESTORE project.

For years, the family’s captain’s licence belonged to her husband. He worked the boat, and Vunisa managed the household. The interest in boating never left her, she said, but the opportunity to captain one herself never came, until her husband’s cataracts began affecting his eyesight, making it unsafe for him to continue navigating the water.

“I had to become a boat captain for our livelihood.

“My husband just had his eye operation last month. He couldn’t see properly for a while,” she explained.

She earned her own licence in 2023, becoming Barotu’s first female boat captain. Until then, she had been a housewife. Today, she is the primary breadwinner for her family.

Kiwa RESTORE Project is the first restoration project Vunisa has been part of. Her role is straightforward in description but demanding in practice: she picks up groups of up to seven women from the five partner villages (Barotu, Naiseralagi, Nanukuloa, Matawailevu, Navuniivi) and takes them out to the mangrove site, where the ground is slippery and footing has to be earned with every step. Once there, she does not simply wait by the boat. She joins the women to plant.

“We walk through the mud … it gets a bit slippery,” she explained.

“Then we plant the mangrove seedlings to the ground – it feels like I am giving back to the land when I plant.”

Although her husband no longer captains, the family’s ties to the water have not loosened.

“Through the money earned from ferrying the boat, I was able to help with the costs that came with my husband’s eye surgery; transportation, food and accommodation,” she said.

Their son has since earned his own captain’s licence, meaning three members of one household, husband, wife and son, have each held the qualification at some point. It is a detail Vunisa mentions with pride.

“My son also supports our house through his fishing trips,” she said.

Vunisa said she was content with where she had landed, though she had not stopped thinking ahead. Her ambition now is to buy a second boat, a step that would let her expand the work she has already built.

“I do plan on expanding this work. I even got new engine for my boat through the money I have earned,” she said.

Beyond her own household, Vunisa hopes her example carries further. She wants other women in Barotu, and beyond, to consider getting their own captain’s licences rather than seeing the role as one reserved for men.

“I want to encourage other women to get their boat captain licences,” she said.

“In Barotu, women are the ones who usually go out to catch the crabs, so it would be good if they could go on their own – with other women.

“I like captaining a boat filled with women, our talanoa, and of course going out to restore our mangrove forest together.”

Barotu is one of five communities in Navitilevu Bay working with Kiwa RESTORE toward mangrove restoration, supported by the Kiwa Initiative and implemented by Conservation International.

For Vunisa, the interest was always there, since she was a little girl on Taveuni’s waters.

And now, she is the first female boat captain in Barotu Village.

item.title: PEOPLE I A lifetime of quiet service
item.description: ON any given day at the Tailevu Hotel, there is a good chance Tevita Matakitoga Cakacakainiusiladi can be found with a paintbrush in hand, repairing a wall, checking a light fixture or making sure the property is ready for the next guest. When this newspaper visited the hotel, he was busy in the maintenance shed, carefully painting as part of another day’s work.
item.content:encoded:
ON any given day at the Tailevu Hotel, there is a good chance Tevita Matakitoga Cakacakainiusiladi can be found with a paintbrush in hand, repairing a wall, checking a light fixture or making sure the property is ready for the next guest.

When this newspaper visited the hotel, he was busy in the maintenance shed, carefully painting as part of another day’s work.

It was a simple scene, but one that reflected the commitment of a man who has spent more than a quarter of a century caring for one of Tailevu’s oldest landmarks.

Humble and soft-spoken, Tevita has become a familiar face around the hotel, where he has worked for more than 26 years.

Originally from Udu Village in Totoya, Lau, he now lives in Nakalawaca, Namalata in Tailevu with his family.

For Tevita, the hotel is more than just a workplace it is where he has built his work.

“I’ve been working at Tailevu Hotel for more than 26 years,” he said.

“When I started work, the hotel was owned by Mr Warrick William.”

Remarkably, it is the only place he has ever worked.

“I never worked anywhere else. This has been the only place that I’ve worked,” he said.

As a maintenance staff member, his responsibilities are varied and demanding.

His work involves ensuring the property remains safe, clean and functional through routine inspections, repairs, painting, landscaping and replacing light fixtures.

Much of what he does happens behind the scenes, yet it is essential to keeping the hotel operating smoothly.

Over the years, he has watched the hotel evolve.

In more than two decades on the property, he has carried out countless painting and varnishing jobs, replaced ageing fittings and helped maintain the buildings as they changed with the passing years.

Each repair represents another chapter in the hotel’s history; one he has helped preserve through his steady work.

His long service has also given him the opportunity to meet many people.

“Since working here, I have met and seen many prominent guests who stayed at the hotel or came for a brief visit,” he said.

While visitors have come and gone over the years, Tevita has remained a constant presence quietly ensuring the hotel continues to welcome its guests.

Away from work his greatest motivation is his family.

His wife is from Ra, and together they are raising five children.

Providing for them has always been one of the reasons he has remained dedicated to his work.

“What I earn from work helps a lot in providing things at home, especially for my children’s education as a few of them are in tertiary level,” he said.

“The money earned has also helped a lot in catering for our daily needs at home and with our church.”

Looking ahead, Tevita is optimistic about the future of the district.

He believes the ongoing development of Korovou Town will bring new opportunities, not only for local businesses but also for the hotel that has been his workplace for more than two decades.

“We are grateful for the development taking place in Korovou Town because as it develops, we will get more people coming into town and more will visit the hotel,” he said.
